notes: Key convention: this file covers BOTH runtimes found in releases.json/gaps.json for this folder -- 'dotnet' (.NET Core / .NET 5+) and 'dotnet-framework' (.NET Framework). Each majors[] entry carries its own "runtime" field. .NET Core/5+ majors use their bare version string as the key (e.g. "8.0"). .NET Framework majors are prefixed with "framework-" (e.g. "framework-4.8") so that a framework major never collides with a same-numbered dotnet major (there is no numeric collision today -- dotnet has no 4.x -- but the prefix is applied to every framework major for a stable, unambiguous convention). OS-support tables reflect what was supported at that major's own end of life / today for still-supported majors, per dotnet/core release-notes/<N>/supported-os.md and the .NET Framework 'versions and dependencies' docs; older Windows versions that a major supported at RTM but which have since aged out of the vendor's live table are called out in that major's os_support string or limitations instead.

milestones.notes: generics, iterators, nullable value types, partial types (C# 2.0); framework-1.0/1.1 had none
first .NET Framework CLR with native AMD64/IA64 JITs; 1.0/1.1 were x86-only (ran under WOW64 on 64-bit Windows)
Task Parallel Library + PLINQ (System.Threading.Tasks); before this, parallel work meant hand-rolled ThreadPool/Thread code

C# 5.0 async/await + System.Net.Http.HttpClient; backported to framework-4.0 only via the unofficial Microsoft.Bcl.Async NuGet package (Task-based, no compiler support for the C# keywords' full diagnostics, no IIS/ASP.NET pipeline integration)

TLS 1.1/1.2 supported by SslStream from 4.5 but NOT the default protocol (ServicePointManager.SecurityProtocol defaults to SSL3/TLS1.0-era values); an app must opt in explicitly until framework-4.7, where the default becomes SystemDefault (inherits the OS/Schannel configuration)

no .NET Framework version ever added TLS 1.3 support (capped at whatever Schannel exposes via SystemDefault, and Schannel itself only gained TLS 1.3 in Windows 11/Server 2022); on dotnet, Linux/OpenSSL 1.1.1+ got TLS 1.3 in 5.0, Windows client support followed once the OS (Windows 11/Server 2022) supports it, and macOS support landed in 6.0
.NET Core 1.0 is the first Microsoft-shipped runtime to officially support Windows, macOS, and Linux from one codebase; .NET Framework never left Windows

SocketsHttpHandler introduced in 2.1 as an opt-in managed handler with experimental HTTP/2 (needed an AppContext switch); HTTP/2 client negotiation became the default handler behavior in 3.0. .NET Framework's HttpClient never negotiates HTTP/2 on its default WinHttpHandler-backed stack
preview/opt-in in 6.0 (System.Net.Quic, needed an AppContext switch and OpenSSL/msquic), promoted to fully supported in 7.0. Never available on .NET Framework
System.Memory / Span<T>, Memory<T> for allocation-free slicing; back-portable to framework-4.5+ only via the Microsoft.Bcl.Memory / System.Memory NuGet package with reduced JIT intrinsics support

3.0 shipped an experimental single-file publish that still extracted to a temp dir at startup; 5.0 made it a true single native executable with no extraction step (opt-in IncludeNativeLibrariesForSelfExtract etc. still apply for some assets)

ILLink-based assembly trimming introduced experimentally in 3.0; became a supported, warning-driven feature (trim analyzers) in 6.0, and is required groundwork for Native AOT from 7.0 onward. Not available on .NET Framework

initial Native AOT publish supported Linux x64/arm64 and Windows x64 only, console/library apps, no reflection-heavy or dynamic-loading code, no WinForms/WPF, no ASP.NET Core (until later previews); 8.0 added macOS and Windows/Linux Arm64 host+target combinations and ASP.NET Core minimal-API support. Never available on .NET Framework or as more than a preview before 7.0

3.0 brought WinForms and WPF to .NET Core, but only as Windows-only workloads (windowsdesktop pack) -- there was never a macOS/Linux build; .NET Framework's WinForms/WPF likewise only ever ran on Windows
first .NET version with a native Windows Arm64 SDK/runtime (Core 2.1-3.1 ran on Windows on Arm only via x86 emulation)
Arm32 (Raspberry Pi class) landed 2.1; Arm64 Linux server-class support followed in 3.0
first version with a native Apple Silicon (M1/arm64) build; 5.0 and earlier ran on Apple Silicon only via Rosetta 2 x64 emulation
Alpine/musl Linux Docker images and runtime builds introduced in 2.1; earlier Alpine images existed only as community/experimental
